purpose: Diagnostic confidence, measurements from different modalities, margin interpretation and uncertain treatment benefit interact. A later good outcome cannot establish that adjuvant treatment was necessary.
source_note: Measurements from different modalities (clinical ~8×6 cm, ultrasound 4.6×3.5 cm, MRI 5.6×4.4×7.7 cm, operative ~4×7 cm, specimen tumour 6.0×4.5×3.5 cm) are reported separately as documented, without harmonisation. prepared_template.title: Margin-negative sarcoma with uncertain confirmation and adjuvant benefit
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his mid-20s presented with a 1-year history of painless, progressively enlarging swelling over the anteromedial aspect of the right mid-thigh. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss or constitutional symptoms. He had bilateral hydrocoele repair in his medical history, no family history of malignancy, no tobacco or alcohol use and no co-morbidities. Performance status was ECOG 1. Local examination showed a mobile, non-tender, firm swelling of approximately 8×6 cm by clinical estimation, with no skin fixity, no palpable inguinal nodes and intact distal neurovascular status.

High-resolution ultrasound at the referring centre showed a well-defined heterogeneous hypoechoic intramuscular lesion of approximately 4.6×3.5 cm in the medial compartment with marked colour Doppler vascularity, raising intramuscular haemangioma versus soft tissue sarcoma. The source notes ultrasound underestimated the lesion because of the limited field of view for deep intramuscular masses, and that MRI measurements were used for clinical staging.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the right thigh revealed a lobulated intramuscular mass involving the right vastus medialis in the mid-portion, measuring 5.6×4.4×7.7 cm. The lesion was closely related to the superficial femoral vessels medially without encasement; the neurovascular bundle was normally visualised and the femoral cortex intact, with no bone erosion or periosseous abnormality. The mass showed avid post-contrast enhancement with prominent intralesional and peritumoural flow voids.

Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy demonstrated nests of tumour cells forming pseudoalveolar patterns separated by thin sinusoidal vascular spaces, with moderate nuclear pleomorphism and granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Findings were considered strongly suggestive of alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS), with definitive characterisation deferred to the resection specimen. PAS with diastase on the biopsy showed focal intracytoplasmic rod-shaped crystals.

Baseline staging: contrast-enhanced CT of thorax and abdomen demonstrated no distant metastatic disease; a subcentimetric nodule (4.2×6.0 mm) with adjacent fibrotic bands in the left apico-posterior segment was considered non-specific, with interval follow-up advised. Screening brain MRI revealed no intracranial enhancing lesion. Staging followed AJCC 8th edition: greatest dimension 7.7 cm on MRI (cT2) and 6.0 cm on the resection specimen after fixation (pT2); FNCLCC grade 2, N0 and M0, classified as stage IIIA.

The patient underwent wide local excision of the right thigh. Intraoperatively an ill-defined intramuscular mass of approximately 4×7 cm at operative assessment involved the right vastus medialis, displacing the superficial femoral vessels medially without encasement. The previous biopsy tract was incorporated in the excision; feeding and draining vessels were ligated.

The resection specimen measured 13.0×7.0×3.0 cm and contained a tumour of 6.0×4.5×3.5 cm. All margins were microscopically negative: superior 1.2 cm, inferior 1.0 cm, medial 1.2 cm and deep 0.8 cm. The overlying skin was free of tumour. FNCLCC grading yielded grade 2 (total score 4: differentiation 3, mitoses 1 (7–8/10 high-power fields), necrosis 0).

Resection histology showed a partially circumscribed tumour arranged in nests and lobules separated by thick fibrous septa containing a rich capillary network, with central loss of cellular cohesion producing a pseudoalveolar pattern; cells were large, round to polygonal with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli and abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Immunohistochemistry showed vimentin positivity, with S100, desmin, pan-cytokeratin, CD34 and CD56 all negative. PAS with diastase revealed focal positivity for intracytoplasmic crystals.

The working diagnosis recorded at this point was ASPS, reached on morphological and exclusionary grounds: the characteristic pseudoalveolar architecture, PAS-positive diastase-resistant intracytoplasmic rod-shaped crystals, vimentin positivity and negativity for all other markers tested were considered diagnostic. This remains a provisional diagnosis; the source itself states the limitations of a diagnosis reached without TFE3 confirmation.

Molecular confirmation was not obtained: TFE3 immunohistochemistry was not performed and fluorescence in situ hybridisation for ASPSCR1::TFE3 rearrangement was not available at the treating institution. The source states TFE3 nuclear immunoreactivity is generally regarded as necessary for a definitive diagnosis, given overlap with TFE3-rearranged PEComa and translocation-associated renal cell carcinoma. The panel also did not include melanocytic markers (HMB-45 and Melan-A) or myogenic regulatory proteins, which would have strengthened exclusion of PEComa and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma respectively.

Differentials were addressed by the exclusionary panel: alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (desmin negative), paraganglioma (CD56 negative; PAS-positive rod-shaped crystals characteristically absent), intramuscular haemangioma/arteriovenous malformation (excluded on core biopsy histology), translocation-associated renal cell carcinoma (no primary renal lesion on staging; pan-cytokeratin negative), granular cell tumour (S100 negative) and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (typical age and pattern differ). PEComa exclusion was incomplete because melanocytic markers were not in the panel performed.

The institution reported that inverse-planned IMRT capacity was prioritised for other anatomical sites and was not available for this patient. This is resource context for the constructed review, not evidence that adjuvant radiotherapy was selected. The board recommendation, any treatment-planning actions, delivered technique or dose and later outcomes are withheld.

Explicit availability limits of this packet: the tumour board's recommendation, any radiotherapy actually delivered (dose, technique, fractionation), treatment response, the later status of the non-specific lung nodule, and follow-up beyond the immediate postoperative period are not supplied and must not be assumed. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. The lung nodule is recorded only as non-specific with interval follow-up advised; no benign characterisation is documented at this time point.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: Any answer must weigh the close deep margin (0.8 cm), size >5 cm, deep intramuscular location and grade 2 against the lifelong risks of irradiating a patient in his 20s, without asserting that adjuvant radiotherapy is necessary or unnecessary, and without inferring benefit from any single outcome. D5b (belief updating) and D6c (sycophancy resistance) are out of scope for this static written task. D4b (trend detection) has limited scope: the only meaningful temporal evidence is the 1-year growth history and the modality-measurement discrepancies; historical slow growth does not establish current acute deterioration, and no D6a emergency opportunity is documented at this elective postoperative decision point.
